questions.text: What does tying the token embedding and language-model output-head weights accomplish in the capstone?

options.A: It forces every token to have the same embedding vector.
options.B: It shares parameters between token lookup and vocabulary-logit projection.
options.C: It removes the need for a vocabulary-sized output distribution.
options.D: It makes the causal attention mask unnecessary during training.

questions.explanation: Weight tying reuses token embedding parameters for the output vocabulary projection rather than learning an independent output matrix.

questions.text: Training loss keeps decreasing while held-out validation loss starts increasing. What does this pattern most directly suggest?

options.A: The validation data must have become part of the training batches.
options.B: The causal mask has necessarily been removed from every layer.
options.C: The model is generalizing better because training loss is lower.
options.D: The model may be overfitting the training data.

questions.explanation: Improving training loss alongside worsening held-out loss is evidence of overfitting and should guide stopping or regularization decisions.

questions.text:
Why does this training loop call opt.zero_grad() after opt.step()?

```python
loss.backward()
torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
opt.step()
opt.zero_grad()
```

options.A: To clear accumulated gradients before the next batch’s backward pass.
options.B: To reset all learned model weights to zero after each update.
options.C: To undo gradient clipping before applying the optimizer update.
options.D: To remove the loss computation from the previous forward pass.

questions.explanation: Backward accumulates gradients into parameter gradient buffers. Clearing them prevents unintended accumulation across batches.
